analysis.one_liner: Lets workers sue in court instead of being forced into arbitration for federal civil rights claims.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees until Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Many employers require workers to sign contracts giving up their right to go to court, sending disputes like discrimination and wage claims to private arbitration instead. This bill would make those mandatory arbitration clauses unenforceable for claims under federal law. Workers could still choose arbitration voluntarily after a dispute arises, and union collective bargaining agreements would be unaffected. The bill was introduced by a single Democrat with five cosponsors and was referred to two House committees, where it died without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by mandatory arbitration clauses—tens of millions of Americans who currently must take discrimination, wage, and other federal employment claims to private arbitrators instead of a public court. They would regain access to a judge, a jury, public proceedings, and full appeal rights. The bill would apply to contracts already in force, not just new ones.

how_it_helps.text: Makes unenforceable any contract clause requiring arbitration of a claim arising under the Constitution or federal law, so workers can take those claims to court [S3].
Preserves genuine choice: after a dispute actually arises, the parties may still voluntarily agree to arbitrate that claim [S3].
Protects collective bargaining agreements, so unions can keep enforcing arbitration rights and terms they negotiated [S3].
Applies to employment contracts already in force, not only to contracts signed after enactment, so current workers benefit immediately [S3].

Amends the Federal Arbitration Act by striking the exemption that currently covers only seamen, railroad employees, and interstate transportation workers, extending court access to all employees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost of defending federal employment claims in court—public proceedings, juries, and appeal rights—rather than in private arbitration, which is typically faster and more favorable to employers. Arbitration providers would lose a large stream of employment-dispute business. Workers would face slower resolution in crowded courts.

drawbacks.text: Employers argue that arbitration resolves workplace disputes faster and more cheaply for both sides than litigation, and that a court-only option could push employers toward more restrictive contracts or heavier paperwork rather than easier access to justice [S2].

Court cases can take years, cost more upfront, and burden overloaded federal courts; arbitration was originally promoted as a speedier, lower-cost alternative, and some employees and unions do prefer it—which is why the bill keeps voluntary arbitration available after a claim arises [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit—ending contracts signed at hiring that surrender the right to a court for civil rights and wage claims—is substantial and restores a right most workers never knowingly gave up. The honest cost is slower, sometimes costlier resolution in federal courts, which is why the bill wisely allows voluntary arbitration once a real dispute exists. On balance the design is careful: it targets pre-dispute forced waivers, not arbitration itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees, and neither took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on June 17, 2005, with five Democratic cosponsors: Reps. George Miller, Conyers, Frank, Markey, and Andrews [S3].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee on the day of introduction [S1].
In early July 2005 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where the record ends [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote appears anywhere in the action history; the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who rely on mandatory arbitration clauses kept that advantage, since a bill stripping those clauses died in committee without a vote.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban enforcement of pre-dispute arbitration clauses in employment contracts

against.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: Committee received the referral and sent it to the Subcommittee on the Constitution; no hearing or markup ever followed

against.what_they_did: Committee received the referral and sent it to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations; no hearing or markup ever followed

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-chaired committees that held it never acted.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to require employees to waive court access at hiring, forcing federal employment claims into public courts with juries and appeals. Forced arbitration's advantages—private proceedings, limited appeal, arbitrator-led outcomes—run directly against workers' legal rights.
Providers would lose the employment-dispute business that mandatory arbitration clauses create, since workers could no longer be routed to paid arbitrators without a real choice.
The bill expressly preserves union collective bargaining agreements, leaving negotiated grievance and arbitration systems intact while workers outside unions gain court access.
